summary: Defines a DHCP-for-IPv4 option that gives a client a list of domain names or IPv4 addresses for SIP outbound proxy servers. It is one of several ways a SIP client can find its local SIP server.

eli5.summary: When you plug in a new phone, it must find the right switchboard. This option lets the network tell it the switchboard's name or address automatically.

questions: how does a sip client find a proxy with dhcp
what is the dhcp sip servers option
how does a sip client find its outbound proxy
how are sip servers encoded in dhcp
what is the difference between enc 0 and enc 1 in dhcp option 120
subtitle: How a DHCP server can tell a phone or SIP client which outbound proxy to use, by name or by address.

tldr.problem: A SIP client in some networks, for example behind a firewall, needs to send its requests through a local outbound proxy server, but it has no automatic way to learn which one.
tldr.mechanism: DHCP option 120 carries either a list of domain names or a list of IPv4 addresses for SIP servers, selected by a one-byte encoding field.
tldr.outcome: A DHCP server can hand out the outbound proxy at the same time as the client's address. The RFC calls this one of many methods for finding the server; manual configuration is another.

today: RFC 3361 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2002. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a SIP Client Needs a Local Server
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is an application-layer control protocol that can establish, modify and terminate multimedia sessions or calls. A SIP system has user agents, proxy servers, redirect servers and registrars.

A SIP client may contact the address in a SIP URL directly. In some circumstances, for example when firewalls are present, it has to use a local server for all outbound requests, called an outbound proxy server. This RFC defines a DHCP option that lets the client find that server. The RFC says it is one of many possible solutions, and manual configuration is another.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a phone is not allowed to call out directly, like a kid who must ask the front desk to dial. This option tells the phone who the front desk is.

sections.title: The SIP Servers Option
sections.content:
The option has code 120. It carries either a 32-bit IPv4 address or, preferably, a fully-qualified DNS domain name that the client uses to locate a SIP server. The byte after the code and length is the encoding byte, enc.

  • enc of 0 means a list of domain names follows.
  • enc of 1 means one or more IPv4 addresses follow.

All implementations MUST support both encodings. The Len field counts the octets after the Len field itself, including the encoding byte.

A DHCP server MUST NOT mix the two encodings in one DHCP message, even across two instances of the option. DHCP processing concatenates multiple instances of an option before processing, so mixing would give wrong client behavior. The SIP server named here MUST be an outbound proxy server.
sections.eli5: The option starts with a tiny flag saying whether the list is made of names or of numbers. A phone can read both kinds, but the network must pick only one kind per message.

sections.title: The Domain Name List
sections.content:
With enc 0, the names are encoded as in Section 3.1 of RFC 1035: each label is a length octet followed by that many octets, and a name ends with a zero length byte. A label is at most 63 octets and a whole name at most 255 octets. The minimum length for this encoding is 3. The RFC says this encoding was chosen to accommodate future internationalized domain name mechanisms.

The option MAY hold several names, but they SHOULD point at different NAPTR records rather than different A records. The client MUST try them in the order listed, applying the mechanism in Section 4.1 of RFC 3263 for each. It only moves to the next name if contacting the first failed, yielded no common transport protocol, or named a domain that client policy prohibits. Several names are not meant to replace NAPTR and SRV records, but to let one DHCP server indicate proxies run by several providers.

Clients MUST support the name compression in Section 4.1.4 of RFC 1035. If the list exceeds the 254 octets one option can hold, it MUST be split as the long-option encoding document describes.

The RFC's example offers example.com and example.net. It encodes to a Len of 27: the encoding byte plus 13 octets for each name.
sections.eli5: The names are written the way the internet's phone book writes them, piece by piece. The phone tries the first name, and only tries the next one if the first does not work.

sections.title: The IPv4 Address List
sections.content:
With enc 1, the encoding byte is followed by IPv4 addresses of outbound proxy servers. Servers MUST be listed in order of preference.

The minimum length is 5, and the length MUST be a multiple of 4 plus one: four octets for each address, and one for the encoding byte.
sections.eli5: This is the same list, but written as phone numbers instead of names. The best choice goes first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 2131, RFC 2543 and RFC 3263 apply. If an adversary modifies the response from a DHCP server or inserts its own, a SIP user agent could be led to contact a rogue SIP server. That server might intercept call requests or deny service.

A modified answer could also omit host names that translated to TLS-based SIP servers, which would make interception easier.
sections.eli5: If a trickster answers the phone's question first, the phone might call through the trickster's switchboard, who could listen in or refuse to connect.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has assigned DHCP option number 120 for the "SIP Servers DHCP Option" defined in this document.
sections.eli5: The official number list now has an entry, 120, reserved for this option.

items.label: Domain names
items.desc: A list of DNS names in RFC 1035 label encoding follows.

items.label: IPv4 addresses
items.desc: One or more 32-bit addresses follow, in order of preference.
